Mixed-effects conditional inference trees on PhyloTree

Source: vignettes/mecit.Rmd
mecit.Rmd

A mixed-effects conditional inference tree (MECIT) is a decision tree for clustered data. It finds splits on candidate variables while a random effect absorbs differences between clusters. This vignette shows why that matters for mitochondrial DNA, using expression data simulated on PhyloTree Build 17.

The problem: same mutation, many clades

Some mtDNA variants are recurrent: the same change arose independently on many branches of the tree. If such a variant changes expression, its effect shows up in many unrelated lineages. But lineages also differ for reasons that have nothing to do with that variant. Each large haplogroup (H, U, L3, …) has its own background. An ordinary tree cannot tell the two apart. It happily splits on clade markers, variants that simply track which haplogroup a sample is in, because they explain the haplogroup backgrounds.

recurrentPositions() lists the recurrent sites, and haplotypeMatrix() says which haplogroups carry them. Back-mutations are applied the way Haplogrep defines them, so a site that is gained and later reverted is not carried below the reversion:

library(dimoose)
head(recurrentPositions(), 8)
#>    site n_branches
#> 1   152        223
#> 2 16311        147
#> 3   146        132
#> 4   195        130
#> 5 16189        118
#> 6 16129         94
#> 7 16362         87
#> 8   150         79
haplotypeMatrix(c("H2a2a1", "U5b1", "L0a1b"), sites = c("16362", "150", "16278"))
#>        16362 150 16278
#> H2a2a1     0   0     1
#> U5b1       0   1     1
#> L0a1b      0   0     0

Simulated data with known truth

simulateExpression() samples leaf haplogroups and builds expression in which a few recurrent sites shift some genes, on top of a random baseline for each macrohaplogroup. Some genes have only the baseline, and some are pure noise:

sim <- simulateExpression(n = 1000, genes = 20, seed = 1)
table(sim$truth$geneType)
#> 
#> mutation baseline     null 
#>        8        6        6
sim$effectSites   # sites that can carry real effects
#> [1] "16362" "150"   "709"   "16093"
sim$markerSites   # clade markers: no effect, but they track the baselines
#> [1] "489"   "10400" "14783" "15043" "2706"  "7028"  "11467" "12308" "12372"

Fitting a MECIT

mecit() takes the response, the candidate split variables and the clusters. The default method is RE-EM with conditional inference trees (Fu & Simonoff 2015). It alternates a partykit::ctree() on the response, with the random-effect part removed, and an lme4::lmer() fit with one level per terminal node. Random effects are estimated before the first tree, so that tree never sees the haplogroup backgrounds:

g <- which(sim$truth$geneType == "mutation")[1]
colnames(sim$X)[sim$truth$beta[g, ] != 0]          # the truth
#> [1] "150"

fit <- mecit(sim$expr[, g], sim$X, cluster = sim$samples$macro)
fit
#> <dimoose mecit> ctree
#>   2 strata; splits on: 150
#>   random effects over 30 clusters; converged after 2 iteration(s)

The same tree without the random effect also splits on clade markers:

plain <- mecit(sim$expr[, g], sim$X, cluster = NULL)
splitVariables(plain)
#>  [1] "489"   "16311" "146"   "16189" "152"   "150"   "2706"  "12372" "16362"
#> [10] "16129" "15043"
intersect(splitVariables(plain), sim$markerSites)
#> [1] "489"   "2706"  "12372" "15043"

method = "mob" fits the model-based version through glmertree::lmertree() (Fokkema et al. 2018).

A MECIT is a key

A fitted tree turns into a dimoose key. Its couplets ask whether the sample carries each split site, and its results are expression strata. The key carries machine-readable tests, so classify() can place new samples from their haplotypes, and exportWizard() draws it:

key <- keyFromMecit(fit)
key$leads[, c("Statement", "Character", "Next", "Taxon")]
#>   Statement          Character Next                      Taxon
#> 1         1        Carries 150    -  Stratum 3: 1.06 (n = 110)
#> 2         1 Does not carry 150    - Stratum 2: -0.04 (n = 890)
head(classify(key, sim$X))
#>   id                     result path
#> 1 s1 Stratum 2: -0.04 (n = 890)   1b
#> 2 s2 Stratum 2: -0.04 (n = 890)   1b
#> 3 s3  Stratum 3: 1.06 (n = 110)   1a
#> 4 s4 Stratum 2: -0.04 (n = 890)   1b
#> 5 s5 Stratum 2: -0.04 (n = 890)   1b
#> 6 s6 Stratum 2: -0.04 (n = 890)   1b
exportWizard(key, "mecit.html")

Random slopes

When a mutation’s effect differs between macrohaplogroups, give it a random slope. The slope variables are also entered as fixed effects, so the random slopes are deviations around a shared slope rather than a replacement for it:

fit2 <- mecit(sim$expr[, g], sim$X, sim$samples$macro,
              slope = colnames(sim$X)[sim$truth$beta[g, ] != 0])
splitVariables(fit2)
#> [1] "150"

References

  • Sela RJ, Simonoff JS (2012). RE-EM trees: a data mining approach for longitudinal and clustered data. Machine Learning 86, 169-207.
  • Fu W, Simonoff JS (2015). Unbiased regression trees for longitudinal and clustered data. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 88, 53-74.
  • Fokkema M, Smits N, Zeileis A, Hothorn T, Kelderman H (2018). Detecting treatment-subgroup interactions in clustered data with generalized linear mixed-effects model trees. Behavior Research Methods 50, 2016-2034.
  • van Oven M (2015). PhyloTree Build 17: Growing the human mitochondrial DNA tree. Forensic Science International: Genetics Supplement Series 5, e392-e394.
